{{short description|Canadian architect (1929-2007)}} {{Use dmy dates|date=August 2022}} {{Infobox person | name = Macy DuBois | image = File:Macy DuBois.png | birth_date = {{Birth date|1929|12|20|df=y}} | birth_place = [[Baltimore, Maryland]] | death_date = {{Death date and age|2007|11|09|1929|12|20|df=y}} | death_place = [[Toronto, Ontario]] | spouse = {{marriage|Sarah Buchanan|1957}} | education = [[Tufts University]] (BSc 1951)
[[Harvard University]] (MArch 1958) }} '''Gazell Macy DuBois''' [[Master of Architecture|M. Arch]], [[Professional Engineer|P. Eng]], PP-[[Fellow|F]][[Royal Architectural Institute of Canada|RAIC]], PP-[[Royal Canadian Academy of Arts|RCA]], [[FAIA]] (hon) (20 December 1929 – 9 November 2007) was an [[American Canadians|American-Canadian]] architect who designed several landmark [[Toronto]] buildings.{{cite news |title=An architect of Toronto; Visionary Macy DuBois loved the city's proximity to the great outdoors |author=Brett Popplewell |publisher=[[Toronto Star]] |date=November 13, 2007 |url=https://www.thestar.com/news/obituaries/2007/11/13/macy_dubois_77_an_architect_of_toronto.html |pages=A10 |accessdate=2007-11-21}}{{cite book |title=Concrete Toronto: A Guidebook to Concrete Architecture from the Fifties to the Seventies |editor-last1=McClelland|editor-first1=Michael|editor-last2=Stewart|editor-first2=Graeme|year=2007 |isbn=978-1-55245-193-9 |publisher=Coach House Books |pages=88–111}} ==Early life== Born in [[Baltimore, Maryland]], DuBois earned a Bachelor of Science in Engineering ([[cum laude]]) at [[Tufts University]] in 1951, and served in Europe and Asia with the [[United States Navy|U.S. Navy]] from 1951–54.{{cite encyclopedia |title=DuBOIS, Macy |encyclopedia=Contemporary Architects |pages=[https://archive.org/details/contemporaryarch0000unse/page/245 245–7] |year=1987 |publisher=St. James Press |isbn=0-912289-26-0 |location=Chicago |url=https://archive.org/details/contemporaryarch0000unse/page/245 }} DuBois retired as [[Lieutenant, Junior Grade]] and commander of the [[Minesweeper (ship)|minesweeper]] [[USS Kite (AMS-22)|USS ''Kite'']] with the [[Korean Service Medal|Korea Service]] [[Service Star|Star]] and United Nations [[Service Star|Battle Star]].{{cite journal |title=Who's Who In Canada, 1975–76 |pages=398 |publisher=International Press Limited |location=Toronto |author=E. W. Whelpton |journal=Who's Who in Canada an Illustrated Biographical Record of Canada's Leading Men and Women in Business, Government and Academia |issn=0083-9450}} ==Career== Uncertain about a career in engineering, DuBois attended an [[American Institute of Architects]] (AIA) conference in Boston, and was inspired to attend the [[Harvard Graduate School of Design]], graduating in 1958. In his final year, he entered the [[Toronto City Hall]] design competition with three other student collaborators.{{cite web |url=http://www.toronto.ca/archives/city_hall_competition.htm |title=City of Toronto Archives:Toronto's New City Hall |accessdate=2007-11-22}} Selected as one of 8 semi-finalists from a field of 510 entrants, he moved to Toronto to work on the second round and, although his design was not ultimately selected, soon relocated permanently. DuBois worked briefly for [[John B. Parkin]] and Associates (1958–59), then joined Robert Fairfield Associates in 1960, which was renamed Fairfield+DuBois when he became a [[Partnership|partner]] in 1962. The firm went through several name changes as partners joined and left, finally becoming The DuBois Plumb Partnership after partnering with [[Helga Plumb]] in 1979 until their retirement in 2001. His first major project, begun in 1959,{{cite journal |author=Macy DuBois |title=Phase I: New College, University of Toronto |journal=The Canadian Architect |volume=10 |issue=12 |pages=47–58 |date=December 1965 |issn=0008-2872}} was the combined residence and teaching facility of [[New College, University of Toronto]], with a curved interior courtyard inside a rectilinear facade.McClelland, page 100 It was well received, winning a local architectural design award after completion of phase II, and is considered one of the finest buildings on the campus.{{cite book |url=http://archives.chbooks.com/online_books/eastwest/106.html |title=East/West: A Guide to where people live in downtown Toronto |author=Klaus Dunker |year=2000 |publisher=Coach house Books |isbn=1-55245-927-6 |accessdate=2010-01-28 |quote=New College, designed by Macy Dubois and built in two phases during the 1960s, was and remains one of the finest buildings on the University of Toronto campus. |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110708141830/http://archives.chbooks.com/online_books/eastwest/106.html |archive-date=2011-07-08 |url-status=dead }}{{cite news |publisher=Toronto Daily Star |date=April 11, 1970 |title=Concern for people marks buildings chosen for awards |author=Harvey Cowan |page=15}} Having been told soon after arriving in Toronto that exposed [[concrete]] "just won't work because of our climate", DuBois determined to prove otherwise in his second significant project, the [[Central Technical School]] Arts Centre.McClelland, page 94 Occupied in 1963, it was an internationally recognized success, establishing his reputation designing academic buildings.McClelland, page 95, photo of ''New York Times'' article, July 11, 1965. [[File:Expo 67 Montreal Canada 1967 (7).jpg|thumb|The Expo 67 Ontario pavilion]] Probably his most-photographed building was the Ontario pavilion at [[Expo 67]], an irregular tent-like structure made of computer-designed fabric stretched across a steel framework. A little too imaginative for some, who claimed the model "looks vaguely like a bat strangling under a white sheet"{{cite news |author=Don O'Hearn |title=Ontario's Whatsit for Expo |publisher=[[Sudbury Star]] |date=March 3, 1965 |quote=The other day they showed off a model of the provinces's building for the 1967 Montreal fair. It is quite something?''[sic]'' It looks vaguely like a bat strangling under a white sheet.}} or "a model of a sort of tent city or a mess of paper triangles or mentally disarranged envelopes",{{cite news |publisher=Orillia News Letter |date=March 4, 1965 |title=Ontario is Just Tents |quote=To protect our readers, we have refrained from publishing pictures of Ontario's $5 million (count 'em) pavilion designed for the Montreal (repeat Montreal) Exposition—it depicts a model of a sort of tent city or a mess of paper triangles or mentally disarranged envelopes.}} it was greatly admired by almost everyone who actually saw it.{{cite news |publisher=Toronto Star |date=April 19, 1967 |title=Ontario's a winner hands down over Quebec in Expo pavilion |author=Ray Timson |page=1 |quote=Ontario has clobbered the bejabers out of [[Quebec]] on the site of Expo 67. To contrast the pavilions of the nation's two leading provinces is simply no contest. Ontario wins it hands down.}}{{cite news |date=April 29, 1967 |title=These are the best dozen pavilions at Expo |publisher=[[Toronto Telegram|The Telegram (Toronto)]] |page=7½}} Dubois wanted a natural landscaping for the pavilion and worked with landscape architect Dick Strong on a design featuring massive granite blocks, of differing size.McClelland, pages 107-109 DuBois went on to design many institutional buildings, including a large portion of [[Lakehead University]], and win numerous awards. Generally in the [[Modern architecture|modern style]], he tempered the [[Brutalist architecture|brutalism]] of [[Le Corbusier]], with inspiration from [[Alvar Aalto]], [[Louis Kahn]] and [[Frank Lloyd Wright]].Jackson, page 247McClelland, pp. 100, 106 To these influences, he personally added sensitivity to the application and environment, building on a human scale, and the use of interior spaces that are useful year-round.Jackson, page 247, "''The work of DuBois...has been based on the accepted credo of the early modern movement, which stressed rational planning, structural order, and a straightforward attitude to design.''" His only significant residential project, The Oaklands condominium and townhouse development in Toronto, is an excellent example. Earning a [[Governor General's Award]] in 1983,{{cite web|url=http://www.raic.org/honours_and_awards/awards_gg_medals/gg-pastrecipients_e.htm#1983 |title=RAIC—Governor General's Medals Recipients |accessdate=2007-11-22 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140502055926/http://raic.org/honours_and_awards/awards_gg_medals/gg-pastrecipients_e.htm |archivedate=2014-05-02 }} the citation credited "Scale with surroundings well conceived; calm of the complex's interior street; considerable value obtained with limited budget.{{cite journal |title=Nine Architects Receive Governor General's Medals |journal=RAIC Bulletin |pages=4–5 |date=August 1983}} As his career matured, DuBois contributed a great deal of time to foster the profession of architecture. His energetic service to the [[Royal Architectural Institute of Canada]] earned him the presidency of the society from 1982–83,{{cite web|url=http://www.raic.org/raic/about_us/presidents_e.htm |title=RAIC Past Presidents |accessdate=2007-11-22 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20071020134829/http://www.raic.org/raic/about_us/presidents_e.htm |archivedate=2007-10-20 }} and he also served as president of the [[Royal Canadian Academy of Arts]] from 1988–91.{{cite web|url=http://www.rca-arc.ca/en/about_rca/presidents.asp |title=Royal Canadian Academy of Arts—Presidents |accessdate=2007-11-22 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928070411/http://www.rca-arc.ca/en/about_rca/presidents.asp |archivedate=2007-09-28 }} His last public appearance was at the launch of the book ''Concrete Toronto'' on November 1, 2007, only a few days before his unexpected death.{{cite web |url=http://www.urbantoronto.ca/showthread.php?p=130028 |author=Urban Shocker |title=Looking for specific architectural details—Urban Toronto Forum |date=2007-11-02 |accessdate=2007-11-22 }}{{Dead link|date=April 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} ==Major awards== DuBois received numerous honours and awards for his work, the most notable being: * Massey Medal (1964) for Central Technical School Arts Centre.{{Cite web|url=http://schools.tdsb.on.ca/centraltech/pdf/commencement.pdf|title=Central Tech announcement|accessdate=November 24, 2007|publisher=Central Technical School Arts Center|author=Central Technical School Arts Center|format=.pdf}} {{Dead link|date=October 2010|bot=H3llBot}} * Massey Medal (1967) for ECE Group Office building, [[Don Mills]] * Low Energy Building Design Award of Excellence (1980), for the Joseph Shepard Building{{cite book |title=Winning low energy building designs |year=1980 |isbn=0-660-50675-0 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/winninglowenergy00cana/page/14 14–17] |publisher=Public Works Canada |location=Ottawa |url=https://archive.org/details/winninglowenergy00cana/page/14 }} * [[Governor General's Award|Governor General's Medal in Architecture]] (1983), for The Oaklands Condominium and Housing Project. ==Projects== [[File:Lakehead University Summer Campus.jpg|thumb|230px|Lakehead University Academic Building (upper right)]] Prominent buildings designed by Macy DuBois include: * [[New College, University of Toronto]], Toronto (1962, 1967) * Ontario Pavilion at [[Expo 67]], [[Montreal]] (1967) * [[Lakehead University]], [[Thunder Bay]] (1969, 1973): ** 20 year master plan ** Academic building ** Athletic complex ** Sciences building * Albert Campbell Library, Toronto (1971){{Cite web |url=http://www.torontopubliclibrary.ca/hou_az_acd.jsp Union, Academic Building, and Student Residences [[Peterborough, Ontario|Peterborough]] (1973) * [[George Brown College]] of Applied Arts & Technology, Casa Loma Campus, Toronto (1974) * [[Ontario Police College]], [[Aylmer, Ontario]]: Master Plan and Teaching, Living, Dining, Athletic and Training Facilities (1976)[http://www.opconline.ca/] * [[Government of Canada Building, North York|Joseph Shepard Federal Office Building]], Toronto (1977) (Federal Heritage Building) {{cite journal |author=Linda Collier |title=Teamwork and Genius Make New Building One of North America's Most Economical and Innovative |journal=Toronto Construction Association News |pages=20–26 |date=March–April 1979}}{{cite web|url=http://www.historicplaces.ca/en/rep-reg/place-lieu.aspx?id%3D10230%26pid%3D0 |title=HistoricPlaces.ca - HistoricPlaces.ca |accessdate=2011-06-10 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120913032136/http://www.historicplaces.ca/en/rep-reg/place-lieu.aspx?id=10230&pid=0 |archivedate=2012-09-13 }} * The Oaklands Condominium and Housing Project, Toronto (1980) * Ambulance Services Headquarters, Toronto (1981, 1995) * Canadian Embassy Complex, [[Beijing]], [[China]] (1989, 2000) * Windsor Justice Facility, [[Windsor, Ontario]] extract: Gazell Macy DuBois M. Arch, P. Eng, PP-FRAIC, PP-RCA, FAIA (hon) (20 December 1929 – 9 November 2007) was an American-Canadian architect who designed several landmark Toronto buildings.
